papers.title: La democracia inalcanzable: Venezuela entre el deseo y el despojo
papers.title_en: The Unattainable Democracy: Venezuela Between Desire and Dispossession
advisors: Robert Weldon, Spanish Teacher, Scarsdale High School

abstract.es: Este ensayo examina los fundamentos históricos, institucionales y culturales de la crisis democrática venezolana, argumentando que el actual régimen autoritario no es una anomalía reciente, sino la culminación de patrones estructurales de larga duración. Sostiene que la erosión de la democracia resulta de la confluencia de cuatro dimensiones: la herencia colonial marcada por la exclusión y la centralización; la captura y politización del poder judicial como herramienta de represión; la instauración de un modelo económico rentista que concentra poder y fomenta la dependencia; y la consolidación del control estatal sobre la información a través de la censura y la cooptación mediática. Mediante un análisis histórico e institucional, el artículo revela cómo estos factores se entrelazan para sostener un ciclo autoritario autorreforzante, caracterizado por impunidad y silencio. Partiendo de la advertencia del ex-diplomático venezolano Juan Pablo Pérez Alfonzo sobre la necesidad de claridad para exponer y resolver los conflictos, se concluye que el colapso democrático en Venezuela deriva del rechazo sistemático a dicha claridad. Recuperar la democracia exige, por tanto, desmontar las jerarquías heredadas, restaurar la independencia judicial, restablecer el pluralismo informativo y reconstruir una esfera pública donde el conflicto pueda ser expresado y resuelto mediante la deliberación, y no por la imposición.
abstract.en: This paper examines the historical, institutional, and cultural foundations of Venezuela’s democratic crisis, arguing that the current authoritarian regime is not a recent deviation but the culmination of enduring structural patterns. It contends that the erosion of democracy results from the convergence of four dimensions: colonial legacies of exclusion and centralization, the capture and politicization of the judiciary as a tool of repression, the establishment of a rentier economic model that concentrates power and fosters dependency, and the consolidation of state control over information through censorship and media cooptation. Through historical and institutional analysis, the paper reveals how these factors intertwine to sustain a self-reinforcing cycle of authoritarianism, impunity, and silence. Building on the warning of former Venezuelan diplomat Juan Pablo Pérez Alfonzo that democracy depends on the capacity to expose and resolve conflicts openly, the study concludes that Venezuela’s democratic collapse stems from the systemic denial of that clarity. Recovering democracy, therefore, requires dismantling inherited hierarchies, restoring judicial independence, reestablishing informational pluralism, and rebuilding a public sphere where conflict can be expressed and resolved through deliberation rather than suppression.

papers.title: A Nation in Reckoning: The Promise and Peril of Indian Unity
advisors: Mrinalini Sinha, Alice Freeman Palmer Professor of History, University of Michigan, LSA Department of History
Andrew Morgan, Research Advisor, Scarsdale High School

abstract.en: This paper examines how British colonial rule transformed India's fluid and overlapping identities into rigid and politicized categories, laying the groundwork for enduring ethnic and religious conflict. Tracing a historical arc from the Mughal Empire through the East India Company, British Raj, and postcolonial India, the paper argues that colonial governance systematically institutionalized division—through censuses, legal pluralism, and separate electorates—turning difference into a mechanism of control. The analysis demonstrates how these structures persisted beyond independence, repurposed by modern Indian governments to manage citizenship, law, and social hierarchy. Drawing on case studies such as the Partition, the National Register of Citizens (NRC), and the Ayodhya dispute, the paper contends that India’s contemporary crises of unity are not relics of ancient religious enmity but the legacy of a colonial state that weaponized identity. Ultimately, it calls for a reimagining of national belonging beyond inherited boundaries, urging a decolonization of both institutions and imagination.

papers.title: Decoding A Syndrome: Uncovering Genetic Substructure in PCOS Using PCA, Hierarchical Clustering, and LD-Pruned Genotyping Data
papers.related_org: Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai
advisors: Kelly Brewer, Research Mentor, Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai
Andrea Dunaif, Research Mentor, Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai
papers.status: Unpublished research paper; submitted to the Regeneron Science Talent Search

abstract.en: Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) is a prevalent endocrine disorder with complex genetic and environmental etiologies, disproportionately affecting women across diverse ancestral backgrounds. Despite extensive research, the genetic architecture underlying PCOS heterogeneity remains poorly understood, especially in underrepresented minority populations. This study investigates the genomic substructure of PCOS within a United States cohort of 940 subjects, which includes significant racial diversity. Utilizing high-quality genotype data, we performed stringent linkage disequilibrium pruning and applied principal component analysis (PCA) to reduce dimensionality and capture major axes of genetic variation. Unsupervised clustering via k-means and hierarchical methods revealed no stable or reproducible genetic subtypes, corroborated by overlapping cluster visualizations. Linear regression analyses showed no significant associations between genotype-derived principal components and clinical phenotypes such as BMI, LH/FSH ratio, AMH, and insulin levels after multiple testing correction. Our findings suggest that common germline variants do not segregate PCOS subtypes within this cohort, reinforcing the polygenic nature of the disorder and underscoring the critical role of environmental and multi-omic contributors to disease heterogeneity. This work highlights the importance of inclusive genomic research in diverse populations and provides a foundational framework for future multidimensional investigations into PCOS pathogenesis.

pcos.title: How the PCOS model sorts patients into subtypes
pcos.note: Illustrative values and dots only. No patient data.
pcos.intro: The model combines a patient's clinical measurements with genetic data to place them in a subtype. Move the sliders, or pick an example patient, to see where they land.

reproductive.label: Reproductive
reproductive.text: Higher LH and SHBG, with lower BMI and insulin. Hormone-driven features stand out.

metabolic.label: Metabolic
metabolic.text: Higher BMI and insulin, with lower SHBG and LH. Metabolic features stand out.

indeterminate.label: Indeterminate
indeterminate.text: No clear pattern either way, so the model doesn't force a label.

pcos.footnote: Genetic data alone didn't separate subtypes in my study (see the reading room). Combining it with clinical measurements is what makes the sorting work.

glioblastoma.title: TGF-β signaling in glioblastoma: the pathway and the genes around it
glioblastoma.intro: Bottom row: how a TGF-β signal travels from the ligands through the two receptors into the cell. Top: genes whose expression rises and falls with each receptor across glioblastoma cohorts. Hover or tap anything.

groups.label: TGFBR1-specific
groups.text: Genes correlated with TGFBR1 but not TGFBR2. ssGSEA tests whether they share receptor-specific metabolic pathways.

groups.label: Shared programs
groups.text: Genes correlated with both receptors. These point to cancer-related programs common to the whole pathway.

groups.label: TGFBR2-specific
groups.text: Genes correlated with TGFBR2 but not TGFBR1: candidates for a TGFBR2 signature to test in knockout experiments.
